title: I Tried to Hack My Own Password Manager
creator: Ravi Menon
description:
Can you actually get into a password manager vault if you steal the file? I tried, on my own vault, with a deliberately bad master password and then a good one.

Not sponsored. Tools used are all free and open source.

0:00 The setup
1:00 A quick note
1:30 Cracking the weak vault
3:00 The strong vault
4:10 What this means for you

sentences.t: So here's the question I keep getting in the comments.
If someone steals my password manager vault, can they actually open it?
Today I'm going to find out, by attacking my own vault, on my own laptop.
The plan is pretty simple.
I made two brand new vaults, one with a terrible master password, and one with a long passphrase.
Then I exported the encrypted files, exactly like an attacker would get them in a breach.
And then I'm going to throw my gaming PC at them and see what happens.
Quick thing before we start, because I know someone will ask.
Password manager companies, including Bitwarden, which I'm using in this video, have sponsored videos on this channel in the past.
This video is not one of them.
Nobody paid for it, nobody from any of these companies has seen it, and if the vault falls apart, you're going to see it fall apart.
Okay, that's it, that's the whole disclaimer.
So, vault number one.
The master password is the name of my dog plus the year I was born, which is genuinely what a lot of people use.
I'm using a free tool called hashcat, which tries passwords really fast on a graphics card.
Now, the vault doesn't store your password directly, it runs it through something called a key derivation function, hundreds of thousands of times.
That's the whole point, it makes every single guess slow on purpose.
So instead of billions of guesses a second, my GPU is doing, let me check, a few thousand a second.
That sounds slow, right?
But I gave it a word list of common names and years.
And it got in after about four minutes.
Four minutes.
That's the bit that should scare you, not the encryption.
The encryption did its job perfectly, it was my password that was rubbish.
Vault number two.
This time the master password is five random words with spaces, the kind you'd get from rolling dice.
Same tool, same graphics card, same settings.
And I'm just going to let it run overnight.
Okay, it's the next morning.
It tried something like two hundred million guesses.
It didn't get in.
And if I do the maths on how many combinations five random words actually have, at this speed it would take longer than the universe has existed.
So even with the file in hand, a strong passphrase basically makes it impossible.
What does this mean for you?
First, the master password is everything.
If it's short or guessable, the fancy encryption won't save you.
Second, turn on two-factor authentication for the account itself, because that stops people logging in even if they somehow guess it.
Third, don't reuse your master password anywhere else, ever, not even once.
And honestly, if you're not using a password manager at all, that's a bigger risk than any of this.
Reusing one password across forty websites is how most people actually get hacked.
I'll put the exact settings I used in the pinned comment, so you can try this on your own vault if you want.
Just make sure it's your own, please.
Next week I'm trying the same thing on the passwords saved in my browser, and I have a feeling that one is going to go badly.
See you then.
